title: Expert hotspot detection and mitigation notes
content:
Summary:

Short: we saw repeating per-layer "hotspot" patterns in MoE-enabled checkpoints and long-context runs across Llama/Mistral/Qwen variants. Hotspots were dominated by (1) sparse routing overhead + memory copies, (2) FFN-expert dispatch jitter, and (3) KV-cache eviction/rehydration latency for >8k contexts. This note captures instrumentation approach, microbenchmarks, candidate mitigations (some cheap, some heavier), and next steps for experiments to validate production rollouts.

Background / motivation:
- Customers are pushing 16k+ contexts and expect near-constant tail latency for chat-style streaming.
- MoE models (our internal 32-expert and open 16-expert variants) show great token-efficiency but introduce non-deterministic per-request work due to routing fan-out.
- Recent outages: increased p95/p99 in Dedicated pools during bursts with mixed model workloads (moe + dense).

Hypotheses (quick):
1) Routing and expert selection introduces CPU/GPU synchronization stalls: host-side routing logic and device kernel launches misaligned with batching windows.
2) Dispatch memory copies (gather/scatter) scale with expert count and active-expert skew, not model size alone.
3) Long-context KV cache pressure causes frequent evictions, leading to microbursts where cache miss latency dominates per-token latency.
4) Quantization reduces compute but increases memory fragmentation for MoE weight slices, worsening copy overhead.

Instrumentation plan (what we added):
- Per-request timeline traces (token-level): host enqueue, routing, gather, expert-kernel-start, ffn, scatter, attention, kv-read/evict, out-serialize.
- Per-layer counters: bytes moved (gather/scatter), expert activation counts, kernel-launch latency histogram, CUDA stream idle gaps.
- Lightweight on-device HV counters where possible (tensor-core utilization, L2 read/write counts).
- Synthetic probes: controlled skew workload where 10% of requests hit a single “hot” expert, others uniformly distributed.

Microbenchmarks (representative):
- Setup: A100s, 2k concurrent tokens steady-state, batch window 18ms, models: llama-13b-dense, mistral-7b-dense, qwen-14b-dense, moe32-13b (32 experts).
- Observed median per-token CPU overhead for routing: 0.8–1.6ms (moe32), kernel-start jitter p95: +1.2ms vs dense.
- Gather/scatter copy volume increased ~x2.8 per active expert slot (measured in bytes moved), dominating PCIe memory ops for our non-NVLink nodes.
- KV cache rehydrate (cold-to-warm) cost: 3.4ms on average for 16k contexts (per-request one-time penalty), with tail up to 12ms under eviction thrash.

Per-model notes (why different):
- Llama (13B): dense runtime dominated by attention matmul for long sequences; KV cache is main memory pressure. MoE-variants (if applied) follow same routing patterns as other models but attention kernel shapes are friendlier to cuBLAS.
- Mistral (7B/30B): smaller FFN but deeper attention optimizations; observed that Mistral's attention path is more sensitive to nvtx-aligned kernel launches and benefits more from longer batch windows.
- Qwen (14B): larger attention key/query sizes and slightly higher KV-cache working set; MoE-analog experiments show similar routing cost as llama but with higher L2 reads.

MoE-specific observations:
- Active-expert skew matters far more than expert count. A 70/30 skew (hot experts) increases gather bytes by ~60% relative to uniform routing, but average arithmetic FLOPS per token remains similar.
- Routing hot-path includes: host-side topk selection, scatter/gather pointers build, and device kernel readiness. Topk CPU sort was a measurable cost; replacing with AVX-optimized radix selection improved latency by ~15% in our microbench.
- Device kernel launches: using persistent kernels (long-running on-device loop) removed kernel-launch jitter but required rework in how we handle variable-length activation buffers.

Long-context specifics (>= 16k tokens):
- KV cache eviction policy (LRU-ish sliding window implemented) caused oscillation with streaming workloads: prefix re-use happens often, but some streaming patterns cause frequent small evictions and immediate re-fetches.
- Proposed cheap mitigation: prefix-aware sticky caching where recently used KV slices for active sessions are retained across short-term pressure windows (configurable TTL per-session). Early microbenchmark shows 20–35% reduction in rehydrate latency in worst-case streaming.

Candidate mitigations (ranked by implementation cost):
- Low-effort (1–2 sprints):
  * Host-side topk optimization: replace generic sort with selection + partial scan (done in AVX).
  * Increase small-batch coalescing to reduce number of kernel launches per token during MoE bursts.
  * Prefix-aware sticky KV TTL (config flag per-customer) to limit rehydrates for chat sessions.
- Medium-effort (2–4 sprints):
  * Persistent expert kernels to avoid per-request kernel setup cost; requires memory model changes to avoid large reserved buffers.
  * Dispatch compression: compress expert activation buffers on PCIe; decompress on-device when NVLink absent. Tradeoff CPU vs PCIe bandwidth.
  * Adaptive routing smoothing: when an expert becomes hot, probabilistically spill a fraction of requests to second-best expert to reduce skew. Needs evaluation on quality/regression risk.
- Heavy-effort (quarter+):
  * On-device routing (move topk to GPU) + fused gather/scatter kernels; biggest win for NVLink-less clusters but most invasive.
  * Model-level expert pruning + distillation flow to reduce active expert count for tail-sensitive workloads.

Quality/regression risk notes:
- Adaptive routing smoothing can alter model outputs. We need co-tenancy-safe evaluation harness: run smoothing in shadow mode for 50k generation samples, evaluate perplexity/response divergence against baseline.
- Persistent kernels require careful memory accounting across pinned buffers; potential to increase GPU reserved memory and reduce effective batch capacity.

Quick action items (next 30 days):
1) Deploy host-side topk replacement to canary pool (Ravi) — measure p50/p95 change across mixed workloads.
2) Implement prefix-aware sticky KV TTL toggle behind feature flag and run A/B on Dedicated test customers with 16k contexts (Sofia).
3) PoC persistent expert kernel on single-GPU node (Daniel) to validate kernel-run loop and confirm memory overhead limits.
4) Add routing-skew synthetic test to CI to catch regressions (owner: Ava).

Open questions / experiments to run:
- How much quality drift if we probabilistically spill 5–15% of requests away from hot expert? (run evals with human subset)
- Quantization interplay: does 4-bit quantized expert weight layout increase copy fragmentation? Need microbench for Q8/Q4u schemes.
- Long-term: what telemetry thresholds should trigger automatic per-customer TTL changes vs operator action?

Appendix: quick traces (synthetic example):
- trace-id: trace-20241104-87ab
  - host-enqueue: 0.2ms
  - routing-topk-CPU: 1.1ms
  - build-gather-ptrs: 0.4ms
  - cuda-kernel-queue-gap: 0.9ms (p95 in bursts)
  - expert-kernel-FWD: 2.6ms
  - scatter-writeback: 0.7ms
  - attention: 3.2ms (long context skew)
  - kv-rehydrate (if miss): +3.8ms

Notes for writeup/hand-off:
- Jira: SRV-1123 is the umbrella ticket; split into topk-opt, kv-ttl-flag, persistent-kernel-poc.
- Add guardrail metrics: bytes_gathered_per_request, active_expert_gini, kv_rehydrate_rate_per_session.
